criteria.remark: Two images, one on each of two pages, carry no text alternative: a large hero graphic on the home page and the account page's avatar. Neither offers any wording a screen reader can announce in place of the picture, so a person who cannot see them receives nothing at all where the image sits. These are the images the scan was able to check automatically; other non-text content on these and other pages still needs review by a person.

Across five pages, 16 in-page links were flagged because the place they point to does not exist: the header's "skip" link targets "#main-content", but no element on the page carries that id or name, and several links in a news list point to a missing "#news" target. Pressing Enter on them therefore moves focus nowhere. That broken targeting is all that was measured; a person has to decide whether another mechanism bypasses the same blocks — a heading, a landmark or a collapsible block. skip-link-works could not look on 1 of 37 scans (the path is replayed once for each rule, and this rule needed its end loaded again); what it would have found is not shown.

Eighteen links across six pages have no text a screen reader can announce. Each is an icon-only link — for example the social media links in the page footer — built from a small graphic that is explicitly hidden from assistive technology, with no label, title or visible wording to replace it. A keyboard or screen reader user reaches these links in the tab order but is given nothing that says where each one leads.

Twenty-four elements across six pages are presented to assistive technology without a usable name. Most are icon-only links, such as the footer's social media links, whose only content is a graphic hidden from screen readers. The benefits application form also has an entry field for a Social Security number with no label of any kind attached to it, so a screen reader user is asked to type into a box that announces no purpose. Other controls on these pages were checked and named correctly.

Ten pieces of text across six pages are too faint against their background to meet the 4.5:1 minimum for ordinary-size text. The grey "Last updated" line that appears in the footer of most pages measures 2.81:1 on white, and the orange "Pending" status badge on the status page measures only 2.27:1. Readers with low vision, or anyone viewing the screen in bright light, may not be able to make this text out. axe could not decide 1 element under this criterion (covered by another element); they are not shown.

On two pages, eight form controls — the name, date of birth and Social Security number fields and the household size dropdown on the application form among them — show keyboard focus with a pale yellow outline that measures 1.66:1 against the white page, well under the 3:1 minimum. That outline contrast is what was measured; a person has to decide whether another visual cue identifies the focus.
